analogy.p: Imagine carrying water in a bucket with small holes from a tap to a plant. The water you pour in is the **total input energy**, the water that reaches the plant is the **useful output**, and the water dripping out of the holes is the **wasted energy**. Fewer or smaller holes (less friction or heat loss) means a higher efficiency. The analogy breaks down because the water that leaks stays as water, whereas wasted energy does not vanish; it is dissipated as thermal energy and cannot easily be collected back again.

bullets: **Useful energy** is the energy transferred to the store you wanted (light from a lamp, kinetic energy from a motor, thermal energy from a heater).
**Wasted (dissipated) energy** is energy transferred to stores that are not wanted, usually the thermal energy store of the surroundings, which becomes spread out and very hard to use again.
Efficiency compares the **useful output** with the **total input**, never with the wasted part.
A high efficiency means most of the input is transferred usefully; a low efficiency means most is wasted.
Because it is a ratio of two energies (or two powers) in the same units, the units cancel and efficiency has **no unit**.
The idea only makes sense because of **conservation of energy**: energy is never created or destroyed, so useful output + wasted output = total input.
Efficiency can be quoted as a **decimal** (0.76) or a **percentage** (76%), and both are acceptable unless the question asks for one.
core.p: Whenever energy is transferred by a device, only part of it ends up where you want it. **Efficiency** tells you what fraction of the energy (or power) supplied to a device is transferred in the **useful** way. A motor, for example, is supplied with electrical energy, and the useful part is the kinetic energy it gives to the load; the rest is wasted, mostly as thermal energy to the surroundings. Efficiency is a ratio, so it has **no units**, and it is the best single number for comparing how good two devices are at the same job.

bullets: **efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer**
**efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input**
To convert a decimal to a percentage, **multiply by 100**: 0.76 × 100 = 76%.
To convert a percentage to a decimal, **divide by 100**: 45% = 0.45.
Energy is measured in **joules (J)** and power in **watts (W)**; always use matching quantities (J with J, W with W, kJ with kJ).
The two forms are the same idea: if a device transfers 190 J usefully out of 250 J in 1 s, it has a power of 190 W useful out of 250 W in.
You can also write wasted energy = total input − useful output, which is handy for finding how much is lost.
core.p: The AQA specification gives efficiency in two equivalent forms: one using energy and one using power. You must be able to recall and apply both, and they give the same answer because power is energy transferred per second, so the time cancels. Always write the equation first, then substitute, then calculate; that earns method marks even if your arithmetic slips.

bullets: For a real device, **0 < efficiency < 1** (or 0% to 100% exclusive).
An efficiency of exactly 100% would mean **no** energy is wasted, which is not possible for real devices.
An efficiency over 100% would mean the device creates energy, which breaks **conservation of energy**.
Common causes of waste: **friction** (thermal energy and sound), **electrical resistance** (thermal energy), **air resistance**, and **sound** energy.
Wasted energy is not destroyed; it is **dissipated** to the surroundings, spreading out so it is not usefully stored.
Quick check: if your answer is bigger than 1 or 100%, you have probably divided the wrong way round.
Some heaters are described as nearly 100% efficient because almost all the electrical energy ends up as thermal energy, which is what is wanted; the wasted amount is tiny.
core.h: Why efficiency can never be 100% or more
core.p: In every real energy transfer some energy is dissipated, most often as thermal energy because of friction between moving parts, electrical resistance in wires, air resistance, or sound. Since the wasted energy is always greater than zero, the useful output is always **less than** the total input. This is why a calculated efficiency greater than 1 (or 100%) must be wrong, and examiners often test it by giving a question where a value was substituted the wrong way up.

bullets: **Step 1:** Write the equation: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer.
**Step 2:** Identify the useful output and the total input from the question; if given wasted energy, use useful = total − wasted.
**Step 3:** Check units match; convert kJ to J (× 1000) or minutes to seconds (× 60) if needed.
**Step 4:** Substitute the numbers into the equation and divide.
**Step 5:** Give the answer as a decimal, and as a percentage if asked (× 100).
**Step 6:** Sense-check: the answer must be less than 1 (or 100%).
Do not round too early; keep full values until the end and then match the significant figures asked for.
If the question gives times, remember power × time = energy, so you can switch between energy and power versions.
core.p: Efficiency questions are mostly about identifying the right two numbers. Read the question and decide which energy is **useful** and which is the **total input** (the energy supplied). Sometimes the question gives the wasted energy instead of the useful energy, in which case you must subtract first. Showing each step clearly is the safest way to secure all the marks, and a final check that the answer is between 0 and 1 catches most errors.

bullets: useful output = total input − wasted energy.
efficiency = (total input − wasted) ÷ total input.
The **fraction wasted** = wasted ÷ total input, and efficiency + fraction wasted = 1.
If efficiency is 0.75, then 25% of the energy is wasted.
In a flow-type (Sankey) picture, the useful arrow plus the wasted arrow add up to the input arrow.
Check: 375 J + 125 J = 500 J, so energy is conserved.
Percentage wasted = 100% − efficiency (as a percentage).
core.h: Worked idea: using wasted energy to find efficiency
core.p: Often a question tells you the total energy supplied and how much was wasted, and you must work backwards. Since energy is conserved, the useful energy is the difference. For example, a device supplied with 500 J that wastes 125 J transfers 500 − 125 = 375 J usefully, so its efficiency is 375 ÷ 500 = 0.75, or 75%. Notice the common trap: dividing the wasted energy by the total gives the **fraction wasted** (0.25), not the efficiency.

bullets: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input.
Power is measured in **watts (W)**; 1 W = 1 J/s, and 1 kW = 1000 W.
Wasted power = total power in − useful power out.
Wasted energy over a time = wasted power × time (in seconds).
A lower-power bulb that gives the same light (such as an LED) must be more efficient.
If a question gives energy for part of the data and power for the other, convert so both are in the same form.
The time cancels when you divide, so you do not need the time to get efficiency from power values.
core.p: The power equation is used when the question gives power ratings in watts, for instance on appliances. Power is the rate of energy transfer, so the efficiency in terms of power gives the same value as the energy version. A 60 W filament lamp that gives out 6 W of light has an efficiency of 6 ÷ 60 = 0.10, or 10%: only 10% of its electrical power becomes light and the rest, 54 W, is wasted as thermal energy. You can then link back to energy by using energy = power × time.

bullets: **useful output = efficiency × total input** (efficiency as a decimal).
**total input = useful output ÷ efficiency**.
Always convert a percentage to a decimal first (e.g. 65% → 0.65) before rearranging.
Example: useful output 520 J at 65% efficiency means total input = 520 ÷ 0.65 = 800 J.
The wasted energy there is 800 − 520 = 280 J.
A formula-triangle style layout (useful at the top, input and efficiency at the bottom) can help you remember the three forms.
Check your result: input must be larger than output, since efficiency is less than 1.
core.p: At Higher tier you are often asked to find the **total input energy** or the **useful output energy** when the efficiency is given. Because the equation is a simple ratio, you can rearrange it with algebra. Rearranging is just doing the same operation to both sides, and you should practise until it is automatic.

bullets: **Lubrication** of moving parts (oil on a bicycle chain or engine) reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated as thermal energy and sound.
**Thermal insulation** (loft insulation, cavity walls, double glazing, a lagged tank) reduces thermal energy lost to the surroundings.
**Streamlined design** (cars, cyclists, aircraft) reduces air resistance, so less energy is wasted pushing air aside.
**Low-resistance wires** (thick, short, good conductors) waste less electrical energy as thermal energy in the wires.
**Better design or materials**, such as LED bulbs instead of filament lamps, transfer more of the electrical energy as light.
Keeping machines **well maintained** and well fitted reduces friction between parts.
Using a **more efficient energy source or appliance** (for example, a condensing boiler) gets more useful output from each joule supplied.
The increase in efficiency is shown by a **higher useful output for the same input**, or the same output for a smaller input.
core.p: The specification asks you to describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer. The idea is always the same: **reduce the unwanted energy transfers**, so more of the input ends up as useful output. That is usually done by cutting down on friction, resistance or heat loss, or by using a better-designed device. You should link each method to the specific energy transfer it reduces.

bullets: Define the **useful** output for the device first; the same thermal output is waste for a lamp but useful for a heater.
**Filament lamps** are inefficient because the wire must be very hot to emit light, so most energy is transferred to the thermal energy store.
**LED and energy-saving bulbs** transfer a greater fraction of the input as light, so they are more efficient and cheaper to run.
**Electric motors** waste energy through friction in the bearings, resistance in the coils, and sound.
**Power stations** and **petrol engines** waste a lot of energy as thermal energy and sound, so their efficiency is well below 100%.
**Electric heaters** are usually close to 100% efficient for heating the room because almost all the energy ends up as thermal energy in the room.
Higher efficiency means **lower running costs** for the same useful output, because less energy needs to be bought.
core.h: Efficiency of everyday devices: reasoning why
core.p: Examiners like you to explain why some devices are more efficient than others. The reasoning always links the type of energy transfer to the waste. A filament lamp is inefficient because it works by heating a thin wire until it glows, so most of the electrical energy becomes thermal energy. An LED produces light without needing to be hot, so far more of the energy is transferred as light. An electric heater, on the other hand, is a case where the thermal energy is the useful output, so its efficiency is very high.

bullets: In a flow diagram, **arrow width is proportional to energy**, so a thick wasted arrow means low efficiency.
Check that useful + wasted = input; if not, one value has been misread.
When comparing devices with different inputs, always calculate the **efficiency** of each and compare them.
Example: A uses 400 J to give 300 J (75%); B uses 600 J to give 420 J (70%); A is more efficient even though B gives more output.
In tables, make sure all values are in the same units before dividing.
In a graph of useful output against input, the **gradient** equals efficiency, and a straight line through the origin means constant efficiency.
State your conclusion in words: 'Device A is more efficient because it transfers a greater proportion of the input energy usefully.'
core.h: Interpreting data, tables and energy flow (Sankey-style) diagrams
core.p: You may be given a table of input and output energies, or an energy transfer diagram where the width of each arrow represents the amount of energy. In such diagrams the useful arrow and wasted arrow add up to the input arrow. To find efficiency from a diagram, read the useful and input values from the labels and divide. When comparing devices, compare the efficiency values, not the raw energy numbers, because a bigger device may waste more energy but still be more efficient.

bullets: Total energy in = useful energy out + wasted energy out.
Wasted energy is **dissipated**, spreading to the surroundings and warming them slightly.
The principle is: **energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed**.
A closed system has no net change in total energy.
Efficiency measures how much of the input avoids being dissipated.
This is why an answer showing output greater than input is impossible.
Link to the next topics: reducing waste saves money and cuts the demand on energy resources.
core.p: The efficiency idea rests on the principle that energy is conserved: the total energy before a transfer equals the total energy after. When we say energy is 'wasted' we do not mean it vanishes, only that it is transferred to the surroundings in a form that is not useful. The wasted energy usually ends up in the thermal energy store of the surroundings, becoming spread out (dissipated), which makes it very difficult to use again.

bullets: Link to **thermal insulation**: lower thermal conductivity and thicker walls reduce the rate of loss and raise the efficiency of heating a building.
Link to **energy transferred = power × time**: wasted energy over a period = wasted power × time.
Link to **kinetic and gravitational energy**: a motor lifting a load transfers electrical energy to gravitational potential energy (useful) and thermal energy (wasted).
Link to **resources**: efficient devices reduce demand on power stations and cut emissions.
Link to **costs**: a more efficient appliance may cost more to buy but save money over its lifetime (payback time = extra cost ÷ saving per year).
Multi-step: find useful output from efficiency, then use it with time to find power or with weight and height to find a height raised.
Always show the equation, the substitution, and the answer with the correct form (decimal or %).
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: Efficiency links the energy chapter together. It connects to **unwanted energy transfers** (friction and insulation), to **energy resources** (a more efficient appliance means less fuel is needed and less pollution), and to **electricity** (power = potential difference × current and energy transferred = power × time) where it is used to analyse appliances. At Higher tier you should be comfortable rearranging, working with percentages, and applying efficiency in multi-step problems that combine it with power, time and energy equations.

exam: **State/Give (1 mark):** quote the equation: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer.
**Calculate (2 to 3 marks):** equation (1), substitution (1), answer (1). Always show working because a wrong final answer can still earn marks.
**Percentage requests:** if the question says 'as a percentage', multiply by 100 and write the % sign; if not stated, a decimal is also fine.
**Unit trap:** check every value is in joules or every value in watts before dividing; convert kJ to J by × 1000.
**Wasted energy given:** work out useful = total − wasted first, then divide by the total, not by the wasted.
**Compare (3 marks):** calculate both efficiencies, then state which is higher and say 'more of the input energy is transferred usefully'.
**Explain how to increase efficiency (2 marks):** name the method (lubrication, insulation, streamlining) and link it to reducing a specific unwanted transfer (friction, heat loss, air resistance).
**Higher rearrangement (3 marks):** total input = useful output ÷ efficiency; convert the percentage to a decimal first.
**Sense check:** an answer above 1 or 100% earns no final mark; check you did not invert the fraction.
**Command words:** 'Calculate' needs working and units where relevant; 'Explain' needs a reason with 'because'; 'Suggest' needs a sensible idea applying the same principle.
**Graphs/data:** read values carefully from tables and diagrams, and give conclusions that refer to the numbers.

mistakes.r: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. Wasted ÷ total gives the fraction wasted.
Efficiency cannot exceed 100% (1) because energy is conserved and some is always dissipated.
The smaller useful output goes on top of the fraction.
mistakes.w: Dividing the input by the output.

mistakes.r: Convert to the same unit first (2000 J ÷ 500 J).
Say energy is dissipated or transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy; it is not destroyed.
Efficiency has no units; a percentage is just a way of writing the ratio.
mistakes.w: Writing efficiency with a unit such as J or %J.

mistakes.r: Multiply the decimal by 100 and include the % sign.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply by 100 when a percentage is asked.

mistakes.r: Compare the proportion of the input transferred usefully, not the raw output.
mistakes.w: Saying a device is more efficient because it has a greater output.

mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction, which reduces the energy wasted as thermal energy.

summary: You must be able to recall and use the equations efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer and efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input, give the answer as a decimal or percentage, and describe ways of increasing the efficiency of an intended energy transfer. It matters because it measures how much energy is wasted and underpins cost, fuel use and design questions.

terms.d: The fraction (or percentage) of the total energy or power supplied to a device that is transferred usefully.
The energy transferred to the store(s) that the device is designed to supply.
All of the energy supplied to a device.
Energy transferred to stores that are not useful, usually the thermal store of the surroundings.
Spread out to the surroundings in a way that makes it hard to use again.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred usefully, stored or dissipated.
The rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W); 1 W is 1 joule per second.
The unit of power; one joule transferred per second.
A force between surfaces in contact that opposes motion and transfers kinetic energy to thermal energy and sound.
Using oil or grease to reduce friction between moving parts.
Material or design that reduces the rate of thermal energy transfer to the surroundings.
The frictional force on an object moving through air.
Shaped to reduce air or water resistance.
The store that increases when a substance's temperature rises.

worked.q: A motor is supplied with 250 J of electrical energy and transfers 190 J as kinetic energy. Calculate its efficiency and give it as a percentage. (3 marks)
steps: Equation: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer.

worked.ans: (a) 0.10 or 10%. (b) 16 200 J (16.2 kJ) wasted as thermal energy.
worked.q: A lamp has a total power input of 60 W and gives out 6 W as light. (a) Calculate its efficiency. (b) Calculate the energy wasted in 5 minutes. (4 marks)
steps: (a) efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input = 6 ÷ 60 = 0.10, so 10%.

worked.ans: Total energy supplied = 800 J; wasted energy = 280 J.
worked.q: A machine is 65% efficient and gives a useful output of 520 J. Calculate the total energy supplied and the energy wasted. (3 marks)
steps: Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency = 520 ÷ 0.65.
